subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: There are four big ideas in the unit. First, data means the facts we collect — and data can be words (like favourite fruit) as well as numbers. We can sort data into groups, also called categories. Second, we count our data, and a tally (a little mark for each thing) helps us count without losing our place. Third, we can present our data — show it — as a pictogram (a chart made of pictures) or a bar graph, sometimes called a block graph (a chart made of bars or blocks).
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Understand that data means facts we collect, and that data can be words or numbers.
Sort data into groups (categories), and say more than one way to group the same things.
Count a small set of data using a tally, and write the totals in a table.
Read a simple pictogram, using the key, to say which is most and which is least.
Make a simple bar graph (block graph) with the right number of blocks and no gaps.
Say why a computer is a good place to store data, and that a backup is a safe spare copy.
Give one way that data is collected for a reason (a form, a till barcode, or counting traffic).

concepts.title: What is data? Sorting into groups
concepts.explanation: Data is just the facts we collect. Data can be numbers, but it can also be words — like the colour of our eyes or our favourite fruit. When we are data analysts, the first thing we do is sort the data into groups. Things that belong together make a group, which we can also call a category. Look at all these things mixed up. Let us be tidy and put them into groups. All the fruit can go here.
concepts.example: All the animals can go there. As they do, keep naming it: “Nadia is sorting the data into two groups — fruit and animals.”
concepts.checkYourself: Can you suggest a second, different way to group the same things? Can you place each item in the correct group? Do not worry about counting yet — that is the next session.

concepts.title: Counting data with a tally
concepts.explanation: Once our data is in groups, we want to know how many are in each group. We count. A tally is a little mark we make — one mark for each thing — so we do not lose our place while counting. At the end we count the marks and write the total in a table. Let us find out our favourite fruit. When I point to you, tell me: mango, banana or dates. Now we count the marks.
concepts.example: Do a real class tally. Show the marks growing.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you count the marks carefully, pointing as you go? Does the total match the number of things? Careful, unhurried counting is the goal. Do you make exactly one mark per item?

concepts.title: Showing data with pictures: pictograms
concepts.explanation: After we count, we present the data — we show it so it is easy to read. One way is a pictogram. A pictogram uses pictures, and each picture stands for one thing. A little note called a key tells us what one picture means. The longest row has the most; the shortest row has the least. Make a real pictogram on the wall. Have them stick their card in the right row, all lined up neatly starting from the same edge.
concepts.example: Then count together to check. Give you a sticky note or card and ask how they came to Ehel Academy today — walk, car or bus.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you count a single row to answer 'how many'? Can you use the key (one picture = one child)?

concepts.title: Showing data with blocks: bar graphs (and a computer)
concepts.explanation: Another way to present data is a bar graph, also called a block graph. Instead of pictures, we colour blocks — one block for each thing, with no gaps between them. The tallest or longest bar shows the most. A bar graph shows the SAME data as a pictogram, just in a different way. We can make a bar graph by hand, or a computer can make one for us in seconds. Go back to the fruit tally from Session 2 (mango 4, banana 2, dates 1). One block for each child. No gaps — the blocks touch.
concepts.example: Which bar is longest? So which fruit is the most popular?
concepts.checkYourself: Can you colour from the same edge with no gaps? Do you colour exactly the right number of blocks?

concepts.title: Why computers store data, and collecting data for a reason
concepts.explanation: Computers are very good at keeping — storing — lots of data. There are two ideas here. First, storing data on a computer is helpful because a computer can keep a huge amount, find it fast, show it as charts, share it with other computers, change it easily, and make a copy. A copy kept safe, in case the first one is lost, is called a backup. Second, data is collected all around us for a reason — a school form asks which club you like, a shop till reads a barcode to know what was sold, and machines by the road count how much traffic goes past. Imagine writing every child's favourite fruit in the whole school on paper — that is a huge pile, and hard to search. A computer keeps it all neatly and finds any answer in a blink.
concepts.example: And it keeps a spare copy, a backup, so the data is safe. When Mum buys rice, the till beeps — it is reading the barcode, those little black lines, to know what it is and how much it costs.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know a backup is an extra, safe copy — not the same as deleting the first one? Can you name one place data is collected? Can you give one reason computers are good at storing data?

debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Data Analyst”.
debugging.fix: Data can be words too. Favourite fruit, eye colour and how we travel to school are all data.

debugging.symptom: A pictogram and a bar graph are different data.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Data Analyst”.
debugging.fix: They can show the very same data — one with pictures, one with blocks. Show the fruit data both ways to prove it.

debugging.symptom: A backup means throwing the old one away.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Data Analyst”.
debugging.fix: A backup is an EXTRA copy. We keep both, so the data is safe if one is lost.

debugging.symptom: You can only group things one way.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Data Analyst”.
debugging.fix: The same data can often be grouped in more than one sensible way — by type, by colour, by size.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Another way to present data is a bar graph, also called a block graph. Instead of pictures, we colour blocks — one block for each thing, with no gaps between them. The tallest or longest bar shows the most. A bar graph shows the SAME data as a pictogram, just in a different way. We can make a bar graph by hand, or a computer can make one for us in seconds. Go back to the fruit tally from Session 2 (mango 4, banana 2, dates 1). One block for each child. No gaps — the blocks touch.

project.title: Unit 2 Project: Be a Data Analyst
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Data Analyst into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data analyst project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I asked 7 friends and made a tally.
My tally marks add up to 7.
I coloured the right number of boxes, with no gaps.
I can point to the fruit that is most popular.

selfAssessment: I can understand that data means facts we collect, and that data can be words or numbers.
I can sort data into groups (categories), and say more than one way to group the same things.
I can count a small set of data using a tally, and write the totals in a table.
I can read a simple pictogram, using the key, to say which is most and which is least.
I can make a simple bar graph (block graph) with the right number of blocks and no gaps.
I can say why a computer is a good place to store data, and that a backup is a safe spare copy.
I can give one way that data is collected for a reason (a form, a till barcode, or counting traffic).
